---
title: Slurm
order: 2
---

Both BioCloud and AI Cloud use [Slurm](https://slurm.schedmd.com) to share
their compute nodes between users. Instead of running a calculation directly,
you describe what it needs, e.g. four CPU cores, 8 GB of memory and two hours,
and submit it as a *job*. Slurm places the job in a queue and starts it on a
compute node once the requested resources are free. This page covers the parts
of Slurm that are the same on both clusters; the differences are summarised at
the end and described further on the page for each cluster.

The work that does not belong in a job is limited to what the login node is
for: editing files, moving data, installing software and submitting jobs.
Everything else, including short tests, runs as a job.

## A first job script

A job is most often described by a *job script*, an ordinary shell script in
which the lines starting with `#SBATCH` tell Slurm what the job needs:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=fit
#SBATCH --output=%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --time=0-02:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G

python fit.py
```

`--job-name`
:   The name shown in the queue.

`--output`
:   The file that receives everything the job prints. `%x` is replaced by the
    job name and `%j` by the job ID, such that each job writes to its own
    file. The directory has to exist beforehand, otherwise the job fails
    without producing any output.

`--time`
:   The maximum run time, written as `days-hours:minutes:seconds`. The job is
    stopped when the time runs out, whether it has finished or not.

`--cpus-per-task`
:   The number of CPU cores.

`--mem`
:   The memory for the job. The job is stopped if it uses more.

How the software environment is made available inside the job, e.g. the
Python that runs `fit.py`, differs between the clusters and is described on
the cluster pages.

## Submitting and following jobs

A job script is submitted with

```bash
sbatch job.sh
```

which prints the job ID. By default the job starts in the directory from which
it was submitted, so relative paths in the script are relative to that
directory. The commands for following jobs are

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `squeue --me` | List your queued and running jobs, and the reason a job is waiting. |
| `scancel <jobid>` | Cancel a job; `scancel -u $USER` cancels all of your jobs. |
| `sacct -j <jobid>` | Show the state of a job after it has finished. |
| `seff <jobid>` | Show how much of the requested time, CPU and memory a finished job used. |

While a job runs, its output can be followed with `tail -f fit_<jobid>.out`.

A single command can also be submitted without writing a script, using
`--wrap`:

```bash
sbatch --time=0-00:10:00 --mem=2G --wrap="python test.py"
```

## Requesting resources

A job never gets more than it asks for, and a request that is too large waits
longer in the queue and blocks resources for others. The aim is therefore to
ask for what the job needs with a reasonable margin, which in practice is
found by running a small version of the calculation first and checking it
with `seff`.

### Time

A shorter time limit makes a job easier to fit into the gaps in the schedule,
so it often starts sooner. A margin of 20–50 % over the expected run time is
usually reasonable. Calculations that run longer than the maximum time limit
of a partition need to be able to save their progress and restart from it.

### CPUs, tasks and threads

Slurm distinguishes between *tasks*, which are processes, and the CPU cores
each task gets. `--ntasks` sets the number of tasks and `--cpus-per-task` the
number of cores for each of them, such that a job asks for
`ntasks × cpus-per-task` cores in total. Getting this right is one of the
trickier parts of Slurm, because which combination is correct depends on how
the program itself uses the cores, and Slurm only reserves them; it is up to
the program to use them.

A single process that uses threads, which covers most Python code, needs one
task with several cores, i.e. only `--cpus-per-task`. NumPy, PyTorch and
similar libraries use threads internally, but they do not always detect the
number of cores they have been given and may start one thread for every core
on the node, which slows the job down and affects other jobs on the same
node. Setting the number of threads explicitly in the job script avoids this:

```bash
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
```

Programs that run as several cooperating processes instead need
`--ntasks`. The most common case is MPI, used by many DFT codes, where the
processes are started with `srun`, `mpirun` or `mpiexec`; which of these is
preferred depends on the program and on how it was installed on the cluster,
so the documentation of the program and of the cluster is the place to look.
This also applies when a single Python process starts the parallel program as
a subprocess, as ASE calculators for e.g. VASP and Quantum ESPRESSO do: the
job still needs `--ntasks` for the processes the subprocess starts, even
though the job script itself only runs one Python process. Frameworks for parallel Python, such as Ray, may likewise need `--ntasks` to
get several workers. Some programs combine the two, with several MPI
processes that each use a few threads.

Whatever the combination, a short test job followed by `seff` (see
[below](#checking-what-a-job-used)) shows whether the program actually used
the cores it was given.

### Memory

`--mem` sets the memory for the whole job. If a job is stopped with an
`OUT_OF_MEMORY` state in `sacct`, the request was too small. The default on
BioCloud is only 512 MB, so the memory should always be set explicitly.

### GPUs

A GPU is requested with

```bash
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
```

and is only worth requesting when the code actually uses it. A GPU job still
needs CPU cores and memory for loading data, so those are requested as well.
While the job runs, `nvidia-smi` on the node shows whether the GPU is in use.

## Checking what a job used

After a job has finished, `seff` compares what was requested with what was
used:

```
$ seff 123456
Job ID: 123456
State: COMPLETED (exit code 0)
Cores per node: 4
CPU Efficiency: 96.50% of 07:32:10 core-walltime
Memory Utilized: 3.10 GB
Memory Efficiency: 38.75% of 8.00 GB
```

Here the CPU cores were well used, while the memory request could be halved.
A CPU efficiency close to `100 / cores` %, e.g. 25 % for four cores, means
that the program only used a single core, and the extra cores were wasted.
Checking this for the first few jobs of a new kind of calculation is worth the
minute it takes.

## Many similar jobs

Running the same script for many inputs, e.g. one calculation per structure,
is done with a *job array*. The script is submitted once, and Slurm runs it as
many times as requested, each time with a different value of
`SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=relax
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --time=0-01:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --array=0-99%10

python relax.py --index $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
```

`--array=0-99` creates 100 tasks, and `%10` lets at most 10 of them run at the
same time, which keeps an array from occupying the cluster. In the output file
name `%A` is the ID of the array and `%a` the task number. All tasks are
cancelled together with `scancel <arrayid>`.

## Interactive jobs

Sometimes a shell on a compute node is useful, e.g. to test a script with real
resources or to compile code. `srun` starts one:

```bash
srun --time=0-01:00:00 --cpus-per-task=2 --mem=4G --pty bash
```

The shell ends with `exit`, which also ends the job. An interactive job
occupies its resources whether anything is running or not, so it should be
closed as soon as it is no longer needed, and longer calculations belong in a
batch job. AI Cloud does not allow interactive sessions that sit idle, and
discourages interactive GPU sessions outside of troubleshooting.

## Useful variables

Slurm sets a number of environment variables inside a job, which the script
can use:

| Variable | Value |
|----------|-------|
| `SLURM_JOB_ID` | The job ID. |
| `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` | The number of cores requested with `--cpus-per-task`. |
| `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` | The task number in a job array. |
| `SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR` | The directory the job was submitted from. |

## Differences between the clusters

| | BioCloud | AI Cloud |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | CPU work | GPU work |
| Partition | Chosen automatically; `--partition` is ignored for batch jobs | `prioritized` by default |
| Interactive work | A dedicated interactive partition, and the [web portal](https://docs.biocloud.bio.aau.dk/access/webportal/) | Idle interactive sessions are not allowed |
| GPUs | A single GPU node, only for jobs that need a GPU | `--gres=gpu:<n>`; request only what the job uses |
| Software in jobs | Conda or Apptainer^\*^ containers; conda requires `#!/usr/bin/bash -l` as the first line | Singularity^\*^ containers, run with `singularity exec --nv` |

^\*^ Apptainer is the continuation of Singularity under a new name, and the two
are used in the same way; an Apptainer installation also provides the
`singularity` command.

## Rules of thumb

- Do not run calculations on the login node, however small.
- Set `--time`, `--cpus-per-task` and `--mem` explicitly in every job.
- Check new kinds of jobs with `seff`, and adjust the request accordingly.
- Throttle large job arrays with `%`.
- Close interactive jobs when they are no longer in use.
